## Starting with predicted probabilities

A logistic regression model gives each individual a predicted probability of the outcome.

Suppose the outcome is hypertension, where

$$Y_i =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if person } i \text{ has hypertension}\\
0 & \text{if person } i \text{ does not have hypertension}.
\end{cases}$$

Let $p_i$ be the probability of hypertension predicted by the model for person $i$.

Consider four possibilities:

| Observed outcome $Y_i$ | Predicted $p_i$ | Probability assigned to what actually happened |
|:----------------------:|:----------------------:|:----------------------:|
| 1 | 0.80 | 0.80 |
| 1 | 0.20 | 0.20 |
| 0 | 0.20 | 0.80 |
| 0 | 0.80 | 0.20 |

When someone **has hypertension**, the model fits that observation well if $p_i$ is large.

When someone **does not have hypertension**, the model fits that observation well if $1-p_i$ is large.

> **A model fits an observation well when it assigns high probability to the outcome that actually occurred.**

This is the basic idea underlying likelihood and deviance.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## From predicted probabilities to likelihood

For a binary outcome, we can write the probability that the model assigned to what actually happened as

$$p_i^{Y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-Y_i}.$$

This compact expression handles both possible outcomes.

If $Y_i=1$,

$$p_i^1(1-p_i)^0=p_i.$$

If $Y_i=0$,

$$p_i^0(1-p_i)^1=1-p_i.$$

So each individual's contribution to the likelihood is simply the probability the model assigned to that individual's observed outcome.

For the entire sample, the likelihood combines these contributions:

$$L = \prod_{i=1}^n p_i^{Y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-Y_i}.$$

A model has a larger likelihood when it assigns high probabilities to the outcomes that were actually observed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why use the log likelihood?

Likelihoods involve multiplying many probabilities, each between 0 and 1. It is more convenient to work with the **log likelihood**.

Taking logarithms turns the product into a sum:

$$\ell
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
Y_i\log(p_i)+(1-Y_i)\log(1-p_i)
\right].$$

The interpretation remains the same:

> **Models that assign higher probabilities to the observed outcomes have larger log likelihoods.**

For example,

$$\log(0.80)=-0.223$$

whereas

$$\log(0.20)=-1.609.$$

Assigning probability 0.20 to something that actually occurred therefore produces a much larger negative contribution to the log likelihood than assigning probability 0.80.

This is where the idea of a **penalty for poor predictions** begins to appear.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What would the best possible fit look like?

To define deviance, we compare our fitted model with a hypothetical benchmark called the **saturated model**.

The saturated model has enough flexibility to reproduce the observed outcomes perfectly.

For a binary outcome, it effectively assigns

$$\hat p_i =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if }Y_i=1\\
0 & \text{if }Y_i=0.
\end{cases}$$

So the saturated model assigns probability 1 to what actually happened for every individual.

Its likelihood is therefore

$$L_{\text{sat}}=1,$$

and its log likelihood is

$$\ell_{\text{sat}}=\log(1)=0.$$

This does **not** make the saturated model a useful scientific model. It is simply a benchmark representing the best possible fit to the observed data.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Deviance measures how far our model falls short

We can now define the deviance:

$$D
=
2\left[
\ell_{\text{sat}}
-
\ell_{\text{fitted}}
\right].$$

The saturated model represents the best possible fit. Deviance therefore measures how far the fitted model falls short of that benchmark.

> **Smaller deviance indicates better fit.**

For individual Bernoulli observations, $\ell_{\text{sat}}=0$, so

$$D=-2\ell_{\text{fitted}}.$$

This gives another way to understand the idea introduced in the lecture:

> **Deviance penalizes a model when it assigns low probability to outcomes that actually occurred.**

A model that repeatedly assigns low probabilities to the observed outcomes will have a more negative log likelihood and therefore a larger deviance.

### Why multiply by 2?

You might reasonably wonder why deviance is defined as

$$D = 2[\ell_{\text{sat}}-\ell_{\text{fitted}}]$$

rather than simply as the difference in log likelihoods.

The factor of 2 is not needed for the basic interpretation. The quantity

$$\ell_{\text{sat}}-\ell_{\text{fitted}}$$

already measures how far the fitted model falls short of the saturated model.

Near its maximum, however, the log likelihood has an approximately quadratic shape. As a result, **twice a difference in log likelihood behaves approximately like a squared standardized difference**. And squared standardized differences lead naturally to the chi-square distribution.

This is why, when we compare two nested models, the quantity

$$2[\ell_{\text{larger}}-\ell_{\text{smaller}}]$$

has, under the null hypothesis and appropriate conditions, an approximately chi-square distribution.

That is what allows a difference in deviance to become a hypothesis test.

So the **difference in log likelihood tells us about improvement in fit**; multiplying by 2 puts that improvement on a scale that connects naturally to the chi-square distribution and the likelihood-ratio test.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why compare deviances?

Suppose we have two logistic regression models.

The **null model** contains only an intercept:

$$\text{logit}(p_i)=\beta_0.$$

A second model includes predictors such as age and physical activity:

$$\text{logit}(p_i)
=
\beta_0+\beta_1\text{age}_i+\beta_2\text{activity}_i.$$

Their deviances are

$$D_{\text{null}}
=
2[\ell_{\text{sat}}-\ell_{\text{null}}]$$

and

$$D_{\text{fitted}}
=
2[\ell_{\text{sat}}-\ell_{\text{fitted}}].$$

Now subtract:

\begin{aligned}
D_{\text{null}}-D_{\text{fitted}}
&=
2[\ell_{\text{sat}}-\ell_{\text{null}}]
-
2[\ell_{\text{sat}}-\ell_{\text{fitted}}] \\
&=
2[\ell_{\text{fitted}}-\ell_{\text{null}}].
\end{aligned}

The saturated model disappears.

So the **difference in deviance** is exactly twice the improvement in log likelihood produced by adding the predictors.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## From improvement in fit to a hypothesis test

Adding predictors will generally improve the fit to the observed sample, even when those predictors provide no real information about the outcome in the population.

The important question is therefore not simply whether the deviance decreased.

Instead, we ask:

> **Is the improvement in fit larger than we would reasonably expect from sampling variation if the additional predictors actually provided no information?**

For nested models, the difference in deviance

$$D_{\text{null}}-D_{\text{fitted}}$$

is the **likelihood-ratio statistic**.

Under the null hypothesis, and under appropriate conditions, this statistic has approximately a chi-square distribution, with degrees of freedom equal to the number of additional parameters in the larger model.

For example, adding age and physical activity adds two parameters, so we compare the observed improvement in deviance with a chi-square distribution with 2 degrees of freedom.

This gives the likelihood-ratio test used in the main lecture.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Putting the pieces together

The chain of ideas is:

$$\text{predicted probabilities}
\longrightarrow
\text{likelihood}
\longrightarrow
\text{log likelihood}
\longrightarrow
\text{deviance}
\longrightarrow
\text{difference in deviance}
\longrightarrow
\text{likelihood-ratio test}.$$

The starting point is quite simple:

> **How much probability did the model assign to what actually happened?**

Likelihood combines that information across the sample.

Deviance measures how far the resulting fit falls short of the best possible fit to the observed data.

And when we compare nested models, the difference in deviance tells us how much the additional predictors improved the fit.

The likelihood-ratio test then asks whether that improvement is larger than we would reasonably expect if the additional predictors provided no information about the outcome.

---

## Can we see the chi-square distribution emerge?

Suppose we generate many datasets from a probability model in which the null hypothesis is true (i.e., $age$ does not contribute to the probaiblity of the outcome $y$). For each dataset, we fit the two models and calculate the difference in deviance.

The distribution of these differences will be approximately a $\chi^2$ distribution with 1 degree of freedom:

```{webr-r}

set.seed(123)

n_sim <- 5000
n <- 200

lr_stat <- replicate(n_sim, {

  age <- rnorm(n, 50, 10)

  # Under H0, age provides no information about Y
  y <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.30)

  fit_null <- glm(y ~ 1, family = binomial)
  fit_age  <- glm(y ~ age, family = binomial)

  2 * (logLik(fit_age) - logLik(fit_null))

})

head(lr_stat)
```

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

d_lr <- data.table(lr_stat = lr_stat)

d_chisq <- data.table(
  x = seq(0.01, max(lr_stat), length.out = 500)
)

d_chisq[, density := dchisq(x, df = 1)]

ggplot(d_lr, aes(x = lr_stat)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 40,
    boundary = 0
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = d_chisq,
    aes(x = x, y = density),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Likelihood-ratio statistic",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 6),
                  ylim = c(0, 1.5))
```
